On the seventh day. This is because of the water judgment associated with the festival. See Taz, seif katan 1, and Tur. Rosh Hashanah teaches, “Pour water before Me,” and we follow the first Tanna that the water libation lasts seven days. Therefore Hoshana Rabbah is treated in some respects like Yom Kippur and in some respects like Yom Tov. The Mishnah in Sukkah, chapter 4, describes the exceptional rejoicing, including the children’s lulavim. All the days of judgment are also festivals, as taught regarding the four periods of judgment during the year, and as stated in the Midrash and Yerushalmi: what nation is like this nation, which knows the character of its God.

Nishmat is not recited. See Rashbam, Pesachim 102b, at the end of the page, beginning “And Shmuel said,” and the continuation there.

Mizmor LeTodah is recited. As stated in Beitzah 19b.

And they recite. As explained above.

They wrote. At that time the judgment of the person is completed together with the judgment concerning water, for water gives life to the world. The Sages said that ten things are called living, and Scripture states, “The shadows have fled,” and “Their protective shade has departed from them.”

In the moonlight. The moon is appointed over the waters, which increase and diminish with its waning and waxing.

Some maintain. As stated in the final chapter of Horayot and the first chapter of Keritot.

And more. As stated in Arvei Pesachim; see there.

Some have the custom. See Magen Avraham concerning the custom in our country, and the aforementioned Yerushalmi that they wear white garments.

They increase their supplications. As explained above.

(א) [Se'if 1] If one is in doubt whether he recited Keriat Shema, he returns and reads and blesses, etc.; because we hold Keriat Shema is from the Torah, and anything that is a Torah doubt; one blesses on it. Beit Yosef in the name of Rabbenu Yonah, Levush, Beit Chadash, Perishah, Taz note 1. And although we said above siman 17 se'if 2 regarding tumtum and androgynus that they are obligated out of doubt and wrap themselves without a blessing (and there tzitzit is from the Torah, as Derishah wrote) it is not comparable at all: there the doubt is whether he is at all subject to obligation or not, therefore one does not bless out of doubt lest he be a woman; but here in any event he is subject to obligation to say Keriat Shema from the Torah; therefore since he does not know clearly that he read, he returns and reads and blesses (until here. And so Kenesset HaGedolah in Hagahot Beit Yosef) see there. However, there is still to question: for it is not comparable to blessing on mitzvot, where there one blesses on performing the mitzvah; but here one does not bless to read Shema, as written above siman 66 note 27. If so, why does one bless on the doubt, since he does not bless to read Shema? Nevertheless, in the responsum of Rashba siman 372 he wrote, and these are his words: "It is still difficult on the words of our teacher" (meaning Rambam) "who wrote explicitly that all blessings are rabbinic; and all that one is in doubt whether he performed the mitzvah; even though the essence of performing the mitzvah is from the Torah, or he is in doubt whether he is obligated in it, like one born circumcised, or on the eighth day of Sukkot when it is a doubt whether it is the seventh; we do not bless at all"; and so he answered the sages of Lunel. And I say: perhaps per the rabbi's view he holds that initially such was the enactment: whoever is obligated to read lekhatchilah reads with its blessings, unless a circumstance causes him, as in reading the Temple; where one does not bless except one blessing. Or, on account of involvement in Torah; as Rabbi, who would pass his hands over his eyes and accept the kingdom of Heaven through reading the first verse; but in another place, when he reads, he must read lekhatchilah with its blessings; and as written: since he did not lose by reading after its time from here onward; as one who reads in the Torah; and they explained what "he did not lose" means: he did not lose the blessings. And perhaps the rabbi learned further from what R. Elazar said: "If in doubt whether he recited Keriat Shema (in doubt whether he did not) he returns and reads"; and since he said plainly "he returns and reads," it implies he reads all its paragraphs, even though only the first verse is from the Torah; and they did not say he should return and read only the first verse while the rest are rabbinic; no. And the reason is: whatever he is obligated to read, he reads as the essence of his enactment; and it seems to me I heard this reason from my teacher the pious rabbi z"l: in returning and reading all its paragraphs, and it does not suffice for us to return and read one verse. And perhaps from this agreement the rabbi wrote so even regarding blessings; until here. And they brought Kessef Mishneh chapter 2 of Keriat Shema law 13; Kenesset HaGedolah in Hagahot Beit Yosef; Orach Tzedek note 2, Magen Avraham note 1; Avnei Nezer note 1. However, Peri Chadash agreed to the answer of Kenesset HaGedolah; see there. And see Yeshu'ot Yaakov and Ma'amar Mordechai note 2; and the practical difference between the reasons; see Pri Megadim, Eshel Avraham note 1.
(א) And if he knows he said the first verse and is in doubt whether he read the rest; Magen Avraham wrote there that it is implied in Beit Yosef siman 40 that he need not return and read; however in siman 64 seif 3 it is implied that he must return (see there; and it seems that initially they enacted that he should return) until here. And Avnei Nezer brought it there; and Razah note 2. And Razah wrote there the same: if he knows he read paragraph one and is in doubt about the second, he must return and read it; see there. And see Ma'amar Mordechai note 2, who wrote that even Beit Yosef did not say he need not return except regarding blessings, but without blessings he returns; see there.
(א) And if it is clear to him that he read the two first paragraphs and he is in doubt about parashat tzitzit and emet veyatziv (whether he said them or not) Beit Chadash wrote that he must return and say parashat tzitzit and the blessing emet veyatziv. But if it is clear to him that he said all three paragraphs and he is in doubt only about the blessings before and the blessing emet veyatziv, he need not return and bless; see there. And so Taz note 1, Magen Avraham there, Avnei Nezer note 2; and he wrote unlike Orach Tzedek, who wrote that he should read parashat tzitzit and not bless emet veyatziv; see there; Razah note 1. However, Sha'agat Aryeh siman 11 wrote like Orach Tzedek: he should read parashat tzitzit alone and not bless emet veyatziv (see there. And although Eshel Avraham note 2 disagreed with Shulchan Arukh HaRav) nevertheless from a doubt one does not emerge; and therefore for practical law it seems he should say parashat tzitzit and also emet veyatziv, only he should not conclude at the end of the blessing emet veyatziv with mention of the Name, but say "Barukh Ga'al Yisrael" out of doubt. And the same if at night he is in doubt whether he said parashat tzitzit and emet ve'emunah; he says parashat tzitzit and emet ve'emunah, only he does not conclude with mention of the Name, as stated. And see Razah and Shulchan Arukh HaRav there.
(א) And if he is in doubt whether he recited Keriat Shema and he knows he said emet veyatziv; Tosafot wrote that he does not return, even when he knows he contemplated emet veyatziv. Responsum of Beit Yaakov siman 135; Avnei Nezer note 2. However, Ma'amar Mordechai note 1 elaborated on this and brought the responsum of Beit Yosef cited above and disagreed with him; and he wrote that only if he knows he said emet veyatziv he need not return, but if he knows he contemplated emet veyatziv he is obligated to read Keriat Shema with its blessings. And even if he knows he said emet veyatziv and is in doubt about Keriat Shema; he wrote that it is again proper to return and read Keriat Shema without blessings; see Shulchan Arukh HaRav. And see Pri Megadim, Eshel Avraham note 1.
(א) And regarding the obligation of Keriat Shema from the Torah; there are divided opinions. Some say only one verse is from the Torah; and so appears the view of Maran z"l in Beit Yosef siman 63. Some say the entire first paragraph is from the Torah. Some say the two first paragraphs are from the Torah; on account of Keriat Shema and parashat tzitzit on account of remembering the Exodus from Egypt; as Peri Chadash elaborated in this siman; and his view leaned that the two first paragraphs are from the Torah, and he brought proofs; see there. However, Rav Shlomo Auerbach siman 2 disagreed with him and wrote that it is not from the Torah, but only the first paragraph; see there. And see Kenesset HaGedolah in Hagahot Tur in this siman, who wrote Yeshu'ot Yaakov (that all these paragraphs of Keriat Shema are from the Torah) see there. And further see Magen Avraham siman 63 note 8 and the practical difference. And although the Sages enacted that one must read all three paragraphs; even if you were to say not all are from the Torah, as written at the head of the chapter "he was reading"; nevertheless there is a practical difference for one who is pressed and under constraint and fears lest the time of Keriat Shema pass: lekhatchilah we wrote above siman 67 note 52 that he reads Keriat Shema without blessings, and afterward when he is free he reads it with its blessings and prays; see there; for if he has leisure he reads all three paragraphs in order to fulfill according to all opinions Keriat Shema in its time; and if he is pressed he reads two paragraphs; and if he is greatly pressed he reads only the first paragraph according to his ability. And further see what is written at the end of siman 46.

And although we said above siman 17 se'if 2 regarding tumtum and androgynus that they are obligated out of doubt and wrap themselves without a blessing (and there tzitzit is from the Torah, as Derishah wrote) it is not comparable at all: there the doubt is whether he is at all subject to obligation or not, therefore one does not bless out of doubt lest he be a woman; but here in any event he is subject to obligation to say Keriat Shema from the Torah; therefore since he does not know clearly that he read, he returns and reads and blesses (until here. And so Kenesset HaGedolah in Hagahot Beit Yosef) see there. However, there is still to question: for it is not comparable to blessing on mitzvot, where there one blesses on performing the mitzvah; but here one does not bless to read Shema, as written above siman 66 note 27. If so, why does one bless on the doubt, since he does not bless to read Shema? Nevertheless, in the responsum of Rashba siman 372 he wrote, and these are his words: "It is still difficult on the words of our teacher" (meaning Rambam) "who wrote explicitly that all blessings are rabbinic; and all that one is in doubt whether he performed the mitzvah; even though the essence of performing the mitzvah is from the Torah, or he is in doubt whether he is obligated in it, like one born circumcised, or on the eighth day of Sukkot when it is a doubt whether it is the seventh; we do not bless at all"; and so he answered the sages of Lunel. And I say: perhaps per the rabbi's view he holds that initially such was the enactment: whoever is obligated to read lekhatchilah reads with its blessings, unless a circumstance causes him, as in reading the Temple; where one does not bless except one blessing. Or, on account of involvement in Torah; as Rabbi, who would pass his hands over his eyes and accept the kingdom of Heaven through reading the first verse; but in another place, when he reads, he must read lekhatchilah with its blessings; and as written: since he did not lose by reading after its time from here onward; as one who reads in the Torah; and they explained what "he did not lose" means: he did not lose the blessings. And perhaps the rabbi learned further from what R. Elazar said: "If in doubt whether he recited Keriat Shema (in doubt whether he did not) he returns and reads"; and since he said plainly "he returns and reads," it implies he reads all its paragraphs, even though only the first verse is from the Torah; and they did not say he should return and read only the first verse while the rest are rabbinic; no. And the reason is: whatever he is obligated to read, he reads as the essence of his enactment; and it seems to me I heard this reason from my teacher the pious rabbi z"l: in returning and reading all its paragraphs, and it does not suffice for us to return and read one verse. And perhaps from this agreement the rabbi wrote so even regarding blessings; until here. And they brought Kessef Mishneh chapter 2 of Keriat Shema law 13; Kenesset HaGedolah in Hagahot Beit Yosef; Orach Tzedek note 2, Magen Avraham note 1; Avnei Nezer note 1. However, Peri Chadash agreed to the answer of Kenesset HaGedolah; see there. And see Yeshu'ot Yaakov and Ma'amar Mordechai note 2; and the practical difference between the reasons; see Pri Megadim, Eshel Avraham note 1. (א) And if he knows he said the first verse and is in doubt whether he read the rest; Magen Avraham wrote there that it is implied in Beit Yosef siman 40 that he need not return and read; however in siman 64 seif 3 it is implied that he must return (see there; and it seems that initially they enacted that he should return) until here. And Avnei Nezer brought it there; and Razah note 2. And Razah wrote there the same: if he knows he read paragraph one and is in doubt about the second, he must return and read it; see there. And see Ma'amar Mordechai note 2, who wrote that even Beit Yosef did not say he need not return except regarding blessings, but without blessings he returns; see there. (א) And if it is clear to him that he read the two first paragraphs and he is in doubt about parashat tzitzit and emet veyatziv (whether he said them or not) Beit Chadash wrote that he must return and say parashat tzitzit and the blessing emet veyatziv. But if it is clear to him that he said all three paragraphs and he is in doubt only about the blessings before and the blessing emet veyatziv, he need not return and bless; see there. And so Taz note 1, Magen Avraham there, Avnei Nezer note 2; and he wrote unlike Orach Tzedek, who wrote that he should read parashat tzitzit and not bless emet veyatziv; see there; Razah note 1. However, Sha'agat Aryeh siman 11 wrote like Orach Tzedek: he should read parashat tzitzit alone and not bless emet veyatziv (see there. And although Eshel Avraham note 2 disagreed with Shulchan Arukh HaRav) nevertheless from a doubt one does not emerge; and therefore for practical law it seems he should say parashat tzitzit and also emet veyatziv, only he should not conclude at the end of the blessing emet veyatziv with mention of the Name, but say "Barukh Ga'al Yisrael" out of doubt. And the same if at night he is in doubt whether he said parashat tzitzit and emet ve'emunah; he says parashat tzitzit and emet ve'emunah, only he does not conclude with mention of the Name, as stated. And see Razah and Shulchan Arukh HaRav there. (א) And if he is in doubt whether he recited Keriat Shema and he knows he said emet veyatziv; Tosafot wrote that he does not return, even when he knows he contemplated emet veyatziv. Responsum of Beit Yaakov siman 135; Avnei Nezer note 2. However, Ma'amar Mordechai note 1 elaborated on this and brought the responsum of Beit Yosef cited above and disagreed with him; and he wrote that only if he knows he said emet veyatziv he need not return, but if he knows he contemplated emet veyatziv he is obligated to read Keriat Shema with its blessings. And even if he knows he said emet veyatziv and is in doubt about Keriat Shema; he wrote that it is again proper to return and read Keriat Shema without blessings; see Shulchan Arukh HaRav. And see Pri Megadim, Eshel Avraham note 1. (א) And regarding the obligation of Keriat Shema from the Torah; there are divided opinions. Some say only one verse is from the Torah; and so appears the view of Maran z"l in Beit Yosef siman 63. Some say the entire first paragraph is from the Torah. Some say the two first paragraphs are from the Torah; on account of Keriat Shema and parashat tzitzit on account of remembering the Exodus from Egypt; as Peri Chadash elaborated in this siman; and his view leaned that the two first paragraphs are from the Torah, and he brought proofs; see there. However, Rav Shlomo Auerbach siman 2 disagreed with him and wrote that it is not from the Torah, but only the first paragraph; see there. And see Kenesset HaGedolah in Hagahot Tur in this siman, who wrote Yeshu'ot Yaakov (that all these paragraphs of Keriat Shema are from the Torah) see there. And further see Magen Avraham siman 63 note 8 and the practical difference. And although the Sages enacted that one must read all three paragraphs; even if you were to say not all are from the Torah, as written at the head of the chapter "he was reading"; nevertheless there is a practical difference for one who is pressed and under constraint and fears lest the time of Keriat Shema pass: lekhatchilah we wrote above siman 67 note 52 that he reads Keriat Shema without blessings, and afterward when he is free he reads it with its blessings and prays; see there; for if he has leisure he reads all three paragraphs in order to fulfill according to all opinions Keriat Shema in its time; and if he is pressed he reads two paragraphs; and if he is greatly pressed he reads only the first paragraph according to his ability. And further see what is written at the end of siman 46.

cases.he_html: משוחררים. לדברי ב"י אף עבדים שאינם משוחררים רק שמלו וטבלו לשם עבדות נמי חייבים בקריאת המגילה ורנ"ש חולק עליו גם הרא"ם ז"ל בחדושיו לסמ"ג כ' דדעת הסמ"ג דעבדים אינם חייבים בקריאת מגילה ע"כ נ"ל בלי פקפוק אליבא דכ"ע שהעבדים שאינם משוחררים אינם חייבים בקריאת המגילה ומורי כ' שאף עבדים שאינם משוחררים חייבים רק שאינם מוציאים אבל מ"מ נ"ל עיקר שאין חייבים כלל בקריאתה כנ"ל:
cases.en_html: Freed. According to the Beis Yosef, even slaves who have not been freed, but who were circumcised and immersed for the sake of slavery, are also obligated in the reading of the megillah. Rabbeinu Shimshon disagrees with him. The Re'em, of blessed memory, in his novellae to Sefer Mitzvos Gadol, also wrote that the opinion of Sefer Mitzvos Gadol is that slaves are not obligated in reading the megillah. Therefore it appears to me without hesitation, according to everyone, that slaves who have not been freed are not obligated in reading the megillah. My teacher wrote that even slaves who have not been freed are obligated, only they do not discharge others; but nevertheless the main view appears to me to be that they are not obligated in reading it at all, as above.
